text: The retrieved set contains little work that speaks directly to the study's hypothesis, which concerns the effect of 32 distinct messages on trust in science relative to a pure control. The closest material concerns how interventions and trials are described and reported, as in the TIDieR checklist, which argues that incomplete intervention descriptions hinder replication and implementation (Hoffmann et al., 2014), and the SPIRIT 2013 guidance on trial protocol completeness (Chan et al., 2013). These works address reporting standards rather than the effects of messages on trust, so they bear on how the 32 message conditions should be specified and documented rather than on the direction or size of any effect. No retrieved work reports an effect of science-related messaging on trust in science, so the search offers no finding that clearly agrees or disagrees with an expected effect. The remaining on-topic items are methodological: CONSORT's pilot-and-feasibility extension (Eldridge et al., 2016) and the CFIR update (Damschroder et al., 2022) concern trial reporting and implementation context. The study's design, a multi-arm randomised comparison against a single control, can speak to the reporting concerns these works raise, but the retrieved set does not establish a live empirical dispute about messaging effects.
